title: Chapter LX

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth asks Darcy when he fell in love; he says he was in the middle before he knew he had begun. They discuss her impertinence. Darcy writes to Lady Catherine.

vocabulary.definition: The state of being ven, level, or disturbed
vocabulary.context: “And if I had not a letter to write myself, I might sit by you, and admire the evenness of your writing, as another young lady once did.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “evenness”: ven (Latin venire, "to come") + -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To rate or value too highly
vocabulary.context: Darcy had been overrated, Elizabeth had never yet answered Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overrate”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The ground where a military display is held, or where troops are drilled
vocabulary.context: Darcy exposed to all the parading and obsequious civility of her husband.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “parade”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Had you not been really amiable you would have hated me for it; but in spite of the pains you took to disguise yourself, your feelings were always noble and just; and in your heart, you thoroughly despised the persons who so assiduously courted you.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “assiduous”: as- (Latin ad, "to") + -ous (Latin -osus, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Promptly obedient, or submissive, to the will of another
vocabulary.context: Darcy exposed to all the parading and obsequious civility of her husband.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “obsequious”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward") + -ious (Latin -iosus, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: At such a moment, the arrival of her friend was a sincere pleasure to Elizabeth, though in the course of their meetings she must sometimes think the pleasure dearly bought, when she saw Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “meeting”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To move away from the position occupied
vocabulary.context: Lady Catherine’s unjustifiable endeavours to separate us, were the means of removing all my doubts.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “remove”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + mov (Latin movere, "to move"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LX,” how does Austen show reflections on love? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LX, how does Austen develop the idea of reflections on love? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LX develops the idea of reflections on love. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LX (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of reflections on love. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LX suggests about reflections on love. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LX to complicate the reader's understanding of reflections on love. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of reflections on love responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LX alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of reflections on love follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LX and its treatment of reflections on love. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LX as evidence for a larger claim about reflections on love in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of reflections on love. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does Darcy's answer suggest about love? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are evenness, overrated, parading, assiduously, obsequious. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““And if I had not a letter to write myself, I might sit by you, and admire the evenness of your writing, as another young lady once did.” Webster's says: The state of being ven, level, or disturbed. Now the word history: “evenness”: ven (Latin venire, "to come") + -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “overrate”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “parade”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Courtship conversation allowed reflection on character. Why does this chapter matter? The answer emphasizes gradual, rational love over sudden passion. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to reflections on love.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “You need not distress yourself. The moral will be perfectly fair. Lady Catherine’s unjustifiable endeavours to separate us, were the means of removing all my doubts. I am not indebted for my present happiness to your eager desire of expressing your gratitude. I was not in a humour to wait for any opening of yours. My aunt’s intelligence had given me hope, and I was determined at once to know everything.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LX,” how does Austen show reflections on love? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about reflections on love, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes reflections on love. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
